A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same compositional ReLU network research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support a reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v2 reports original function-approximation experiments, including minimum and mean MSE across 30 models in Tables 1–2 and network behavior analyses.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds sparse-data training with evaluation on unseen points in Table 3 and Figure 4.

M1.justification: The four-neuron compositional architecture, trainable triangle peaks, differentiability scaling rule, and pretraining followed by ordinary weight optimization remain unchanged. Appendix 7.1 documents this existing procedure with matrices and pseudocode.

E1.justification: Both evaluate the same four synthetic one-dimensional curves: x^3, x^11, sine, and tanh(3x). The added sparse-data experiment changes sampling and held-out evaluation within this retained coverage.

E2.justification: Tables 1–2 retain Default Network, RAAI Distribution, and the same pretraining variants; 'No Pretraining' becomes 'Pretraining Skipped.' The new sparse-data comparison uses the already evaluated default network without changing membership in the existing comparisons.

E3.justification: v2 evaluates fitting to 500 evenly spaced points without a train-test split. v3 retains that experiment and adds a protocol with 10 training points and 10 interleaved test points. The existing architecture, optimizer, and MSE metric remain.

E4.justification: v3 adds a focused analysis of generalization under sparse training, testing whether additional linear regions improve predictions between observed points. Table 3 and Figure 4 supplement the retained pretraining ablations and internal-network case studies.

E5.justification: Both retain the 30-model protocol and minimum/mean summaries for Tables 1–2. Neither reports seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Table 3 adds minimum errors without introducing a new uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: All numerical entries in Tables 1–2 remain unchanged. New Table 3 reports lower minimum test MSE for differentiable pretraining on all four curves; for x^3, it reports 5.65e-6 versus 2.41e-4 for the default network. These are new sparse-protocol results, not improvements over v2 under identical conditions.

T1.justification: Beyond relocating proofs, v3 revises first-derivative statements from continuity to existence and explicitly includes the scaling condition in the sufficiency theorem. Appendix 7.6 adds a limiting argument to the convexity proof, and 7.4 replaces v2's maximum-error argument with geometric-tail reasoning. The second-derivative derivation also corrects slope signs. These refine the existing theoretical framework.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain reparameterization, two-stage training, and substantially better approximation of convex one-dimensional functions. v3 explicitly includes that restriction in the abstract, but it was already stated in v2's introduction and conclusion.

C2.justification: v3 interprets the sparse-data results as evidence that additional linear regions capture underlying nonlinearity and improve prediction even when regions outnumber observations. Section 5 also softens 'only suitable' for convex functions to 'only guaranteed to be suitable'; the principal limitations remain.

D1.justification: v3 newly discloses Adam's learning rate of 0.0001. Appendix 7.1 supplies explicit layer matrices, backpropagation-through-initialization pseudocode, and clarification that each training phase runs for 1,000 epochs. These are documentation additions, not established changes to the existing experiments.

R1.justification: The cited works and substantive positioning remain the same: extending triangle-wave approximation constructions and addressing limitations of random initialization. Expanded author names and citation formatting do not introduce new related work.

P1.justification: v3 substantially reorganizes the exposition by moving the main differentiability derivation into Appendix 7.2, condensing Section 3.1, and restructuring the appendix. It also rewrites substantial explanatory passages concerning network construction, training motivation, and experimental interpretation.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to a single-column layout with wrapped figures. Figure 2 is rearranged horizontally; Table 3 and Figures 4 and 8 are added. v2's Figure 4 moves to the appendix as Figure 7, while existing result plots are retained and resized.

improvement.justification: v3 strengthens v2's dense-fitting evidence with held-out interpolation results and improves reproducibility through the learning rate, explicit training matrices, and per-phase budget. These are useful gains, although evaluation remains confined to the same simple curves and the new comparison reports only minimum errors.
